chapter: Paris, the Blackbirds and Noble Sissle
title: Labor permits, the French union and replacing the bandsmen
summary: At La Vie Pallem the union tried to oust his foreign players; Briggs, who held a labor permit, replaced the uncovered men with the proprietor's backing and finished his contract.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Yeh, right. And that's where I worked with an orchestra and had difficulties with the French Union, 'cause we were all foreigners.
Right.
Fortunately, I personally did not have any worry, because
Briggs
when I came to France the first thing that I did was to try to abide with the law. I knew you had to -- if you came to work, in anybody's country, you should ask for a labor permit.
Right.

And that's what I did, when I came to France, I asked for a labor permit, and I was given my card, and I had no difficulties myself, but my drummer and piano player who was a Belgian, he figured, he said, 'Well, I'm considered French, and I don't have to have a labor permit,' and he was wrong.
And our drummer, who was a Hungarian, I knew he would have difficulties. He had difficulties.

But the thing is, the Union, we had a bunch of guys who were more or less politicians and musicians in the Union, and bad musicians, very bad musicians, and they tried to get me thrown out, but my contract
Briggs 195
was solid, and the managing director of the La Vie Pellam (?) told them, 'cause he came one evening to examine papers to see whether everyone was in order or not.
And quite a few of the boys were not in order, so I told him, I said, -- you know Place Pigalle at all?
A little bit. I've been around there.
You know there's a tobacco shop.
Yes.
That I told the boys after they check up, and a few of them were not in order, I said, "Just hang around that café until we're through," --
So, during the check up, Mr. -- I'm trying to -- I must call him Mister. They were two brothers, the proprietors.
In any case, the proprietor said -- after check up, he told the guy from the Union, from the local, he said -- ah, yes,
Briggs 196
my orchestra is waiting over there at the café to come in right away," he said, "They'll wait an awfully long while."
He said, "Mr. Briggs, you replace the men that are not in order, and you continue the contract tomorrow, but don't take any men from the Union."
Now, I was more or less new in Paris, and I really didn't know, what's what, who was what?
Right.
So I went over to the café after work, and my boys were all there having supper together, and I -- there's one fine boy that I still see today, George Marion, a wonderful drummer.
Marion, his name is?
Marion.
Marion, right.
Marion, M-a-r-i-o-n.
He said to me, in French, he said, "J'ai ont
Briggs

bete, huh." 'Je dit, yes, I said. He said, you have some word, and I said, "Yeh." He said, "C'est Jean Berson qu'il a fait, ca." Jean Berson is one of the worst trumpet players, the world's worst, -- there are two brothers.
Yeh.

You see, but he was a big shot in the Union. Jean Berson. I said, "I know". I read eyes, because the Inspector said, that a band was waiting in here, in Tababelle, to come to replace us. And he said, "Oh, you don't have to worry about that." I said, "No, I don't have to worry, because Mr. --". Oh, I can't remember, it's so stupid.
Yeh, the proprietor.
The proprietor told me to replace those men but don't bring me any Union men. I said, "But I don't know how to
Briggs

navigate." I said, "Maybe you can help me." He said, "Me, yeh, sure, sure." He said, "I'll call you tomorrow morning." He said, "I'll call you tomorrow morning and make arrangements to meet the men, in the afternoon at the same Cafe Belle." And that's what happened.
So you got --
The men I needed.
So I continued, I finished my contract, but after my contract, that same guy tried to get the job.
Right.
